extracted.intended_audience: novelists, creative-writing students, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on selecting and handling narrative method (first‑person, third‑person, epistolary, etc.) to best render characters, especially when a story's centre of gravity is a mind rather than external events. Explains when to dramatize a consciousness and how to preserve pictorial freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of the first‑person/autobiographic narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: First‑person narration is effective when the story is largely a picture of life beyond the narrator — when the narrator 'tells' and supplies the scene — but is limited when the story's centre of gravity lies in the narrator's own inner life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use first person when you need a named teller to lend authority and to describe a broad external world (examples: Dickens, Thackeray). Avoid it when the plot requires a searching, dramatic portrait of the narrator's consciousness; the autobiographer can only 'report' himself and may be 'overtaxed' if the subject demands the dramatization of his inner life (example: Meredith's Harry Richmond).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize a character's mind when the mind is the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: When the main weight of attention is claimed by a character's own consciousness (the 'leading event' is himself), the inner life should be rendered as drama rather than as retrospective report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer techniques that make the mind 'tell its own story' in action (example: Henry James's Strether, Dostoevsky's Raskolnikov). Present thought as it proceeds—its impulses and reactions—so the reader experiences the change rather than merely reads an account of it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of third‑person (or indirect) methods to show thought in action
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than reverting to an author's summary or a narrator's retrospective report, the novelist can place the reader in front of a character's mental activity by showing the mind at work in the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shift from 'receiving his report' to 'seeing him in the act of judging and reflecting' so the character's consciousness becomes a visible dramatic fact on the page (example: The Ambassadors as contrasted with autobiographical narration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of method (push method only as far as the subject profits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author should advance narrative method toward drama only as far as the subject benefits; over‑treatment harms a story as much as inadequate treatment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide the 'ideal point' along the line from pictorial/reporting to full dramatization by asking whether further dramatization would illuminate the subject or merely displace it (example: David Copperfield would not gain by making David's mind the dramatic foreground).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not let the narrator stand between reader and active mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid a situation where the hero or heroine 'comes between us and his active mind' by posing as both describer and chief subject; this weakens immediate dramatic impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the emotional core of the book is the character's inner life, do not allow that character to remain merely the reporter of events; either dramatize the inner life or choose another vantage point that exposes it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer drama ('showing') where living drama is possible
rubrics_metrics.description: 'No reflection, no picture, where living drama is possible' — showing action or the mind in action is generally superior to reflective summarization when the scene or consciousness can be made immediate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When you can stage feelings, thoughts, or events so they make their own impression, do so; reserve reflective or pictorial modes for material that cannot profit from dramatic immediacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the novelist's pictorial freedom while dramatizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Dramatizing a mind does not force the novelist to abandon panoramic description or summary; the mind, once visible, can still 'lend us eyes' and produce broad vision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can dramatize internal life and yet retain the capacity for extended, panoramic commentary—the scale and economy of expression will differ (e.g., Strether imparts summaries with 'a word barely breathed' where Thackeray uses sweeping surveys).

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistolary/diary method to capture contemporaneous emotion
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters or a running diary may dramatize sensibility by keeping a character's emotions in the foreground as they occur (example: Richardson's Clarissa), producing immediacy and recurring suspense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use epistolary form when the subject is the character's present emotion or comportment under strain. Beware the contrivances required to preserve verisimilitude (keeping people at a distance so communication is only by letter) and practical limits on plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent thought by its observable 'look and behaviour'
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of explaining what a character thinks, the novelist can render the movement and behaviour of thought—its impulses, flickers, and reactions—as the material of drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat mental impulses as players on a stage: let their bearing and behaviour imply inward states so that the reader infers interiority from the mind's surface movements (explicitly advocated in The Ambassadors).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain verisimilitude: a credible account must detach its subject for inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: A first‑person account of oneself is inherently limited—'no man can completely objectify himself'—so credibility often requires methods that let the reader judge independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When accuracy or objectivity about inner states is essential, prefer dramatization or an external vantage that detaches the experience for inspection rather than relying solely on the narrator's retrospective account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial withdrawal/indirectness to achieve a straighter effect
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'indirect' method—author standing aside so the thing itself is in view—often produces a 'straighter' and more effective impression for the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remove obtrusive interpretation where possible. Let characters' actions, the dramatized mind, and the scene communicate meaning rather than having the author explicitly explain it; indirectness can bring the reader nearer to experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage progression: use successive methods as the novel requires
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a natural progression of modes—simple storyteller, autobiographical narrator, then dramatization of mind—each appropriate to different subjects and emphases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the progression as a tool: begin with pictorial description if needed, and advance toward dramatization when the subject demands visibility of thought. Choose the point that best serves the story's central matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of the practical costs of methods that dramatize mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Some methods (e.g., epistolary) gain intimacy at the cost of narrative plausibility or logistical strain; likewise, trying to have a narrator both report and be the dramatic centre can be an impossible demand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the tradeoffs: immediacy versus plausibility, panoramic survey versus concentrated interiority. If a chosen method imposes improbable contrivances or overburdens the narrator, reconsider the approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shift point of view artfully when necessary to place reader advantageously
rubrics_metrics.description: Point‑of‑view shifts can position the reader in a better place to understand a character's history or transformation, but must be contrived so the reader is not unduly aware of the trick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you shift vantage (as in The Ambassadors), do so subtly and for a clear purpose—to give the reader access to material the protagonist cannot fully grasp. Ensure the shift enhances rather than confuses the reader's sense of immediacy.
